paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 2021, two billionaires flew to the edge of space within nine days of each other, and the era of space tourism was declared open. Tickets cost between several hundred thousand and tens of millions of dollars, so for now only the very rich can afford them. Supporters say that the industry will follow the path of aviation, becoming cheaper and safer over time. I am not convinced that the comparison is fair, and I believe that the case for developing space tourism is weaker than its promoters admit.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Consider the environmental cost. A single rocket launch releases large amounts of carbon dioxide and black soot directly into the upper atmosphere, where its effects may last far longer than emissions released near the ground. Passengers on a short suborbital flight are estimated to be responsible for as much carbon as an average person produces in several months. Defenders point out that the total number of flights is tiny compared with aviation. That is true today, but the companies' business plans assume rapid growth.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is also a question of priorities. Money invested in space tourism could, in theory, support scientific missions, but the reality is that most of it comes from private investors seeking a return. Supporters claim that tourism will pay for technology that benefits everyone, as military spending has often done. Perhaps so, but the same funds could be used to tackle problems with a more direct effect on human lives, such as clean water or climate change.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: On the other hand, I admit there are arguments in favour. Seeing the Earth from space has a powerful effect on those who experience it, a phenomenon astronauts call the overview effect. Many return with a stronger sense of the planet's fragility. If more people had that experience, it might change attitudes. Yet it is hard to imagine that a few minutes of weightlessness for a small group of millionaires would have a wider impact on public opinion.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Should space tourism be banned? No, I would not go that far. Private companies have reduced the cost of launches significantly, and some of their technology has useful applications. But governments should require operators to report their emissions, set safety standards and consider taxing flights. If it is going to be a luxury, then those who can afford it should pay the full cost, including the cost to the planet.
